Eulachon (Thaleichthys pacificus) eggs, once fertilized, develop within a transparent chorion and hatch as yolk-sac larvae that depend entirely on endogenous reserves. The average wet weight at birth for a newly emerged prolarva is approximately 0.000449 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000449 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of this species. This lecithotrophic stage persists until the yolk is fully absorbed and the mouth opens, at which point the larva must successfully capture its first exogenous prey to avoid starvation. During this early phase, water temperature plays a critical role in developmental rate. Growth trajectories from the yolk-sac larva through the juvenile stage are strongly influenced by thermal conditions; field records indicate that individuals reared at a stable water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C] exhibit a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days]. This longevity is relatively modest compared to other osmerids and likely reflects the species' semelparous reproductive strategy and the high energetic demands of its anadromous migration.

As juveniles transition toward the sub-adult phase, they undergo significant somatic growth in estuarine and nearshore marine environments before initiating their spawning migration. The total length at which individuals become reproductively mature, marking the onset of puberty, is approximately 15.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15.5 centimeters]. This measurement represents a critical inflection point in the life cycle, as fish below this size rarely exhibit developed gonads during the upstream spawning run. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from length-weight regressions, is about 22.5 grams [Wwp = about 22.5 grams], indicating that substantial mass gain must occur during the marine feeding phase before energy can be allocated to gamete production. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults can reach approximately 269 grams [Wwi = approximately 269 grams], a value associated with the largest individuals recorded in spawning populations. This asymptotic body size reflects the upper limit of growth attainable under optimal foraging conditions in the Gulf of Alaska and adjacent waters.

Reproductive output in Thaleichthys pacificus is tightly coupled to female body size and the environmental conditions encountered during the prespawning period. Under the thermal regime characteristic of their natal streams during the spawning season (9 °C [T = 9 °C]), females have been observed to deposit between 20,000 and 60,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 20,000 and 60,000 eggs per spawning event]. Because this species is semelparous, each female spawns only once in her lifetime, yielding a reproductive frequency of one spawning event per lifetime [F_R_i = one spawning event per lifetime]. This single, massive reproductive effort places considerable physiological strain on the individual, and post-spawning mortality is nearly universal. The combination of high fecundity and obligate semelparity means that annual recruitment is highly variable and depends almost entirely on the survival of eggs and larvae during the incubation and early rearing periods within the freshwater spawning habitat.

The maximum total length recorded for Thaleichthys pacificus in surveyed spawning runs is 34 centimeters [Li = 34 centimeters], a size attained by a small fraction of older individuals that have enjoyed exceptionally favorable marine feeding conditions. This ultimate length serves as a useful benchmark for assessing population condition and growth potential, as it represents the upper boundary of the species' size range in the wild. In comparison with the length at puberty of 15.5 centimeters [Lp = 15.5 centimeters], the trajectory from puberty to maximum size involves an approximately twofold increase in linear dimension, while the corresponding increase in wet weight from 22.5 grams [Wwp = 22.5 grams] to 269 grams [Wwi = 269 grams] is more than tenfold, reflecting the strongly allometric relationship between length and mass in this species. Such substantial post-pubertal growth is somewhat unusual among semelparous fishes, which typically channel most available energy into gonadal development rather than continued somatic expansion once maturity is reached. The lifespan of the species, at roughly 5 years, aligns with the pattern observed in many other semelparous osmerids of comparable body size, highlighting a consistent life history strategy across the family.

Life-history theory predicts that semelparous species such as Eulachon should exhibit a relatively short maximum lifespan, and empirical data support this expectation. Under the thermal conditions prevailing in their natal streams at 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This duration encompasses the entire period from egg fertilisation through the juvenile marine feeding stage, the adult spawning migration, and eventual post-reproductive death. Interestingly, the lifespan of about 5 years is comparable to that of other anadromous osmerids of similar body size, suggesting a conserved life-history pace within the family. This fast-lived strategy, coupled with a single, massive reproductive event, allows Thaleichthys pacificus to optimize its fitness within the constraints of its seasonal, high-latitude environment. The ultimate size, represented by a total length of 34 centimeters, further positions this species within the typical range for its genus.
